description: We are a creative team in NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026 building “Left Behind: NASA’s Forgotten Machines,” an interactive story of abandoned equipment on the Moon and Mars. We love space, technology and storytelling. We welcome teammates skilled in web development, 3D design, UI/UX, NASA data research or scientific visualization who want to help create an engaging space exploration experience.
summary:
Left Behind: NASA's Forgotten Machines is an interactive 3D storytelling website about the equipment NASA has left on the Moon and Mars. Most people never read NASA's technical mission pages, and the word "abandoned" makes these machines sound like dead junk. We built Left Behind for students and curious people with no space background, to show that abandoned does not mean forgotten.

Visitors spin 3D models of the Sun, Moon and Mars, tap glowing dots on real landing sites, and learn what each spacecraft, rover and instrument measured. Every machine is marked active, dormant or unknown, so "abandoned" becomes a status, not an ending. Interactive charts compare the planned and actual lifespans of Mars rovers, and a distance slider shows how far Voyager 1 has travelled.

The project addresses the challenge by turning overlooked mission records into a story anyone can explore, in plain words and at their own pace. It matters because it makes complex space science accessible and shows that even forgotten machines keep contributing to scientific knowledge. Built with HTML, CSS, JavaScript and Three.js, using public NASA mission records.
details:
WHAT IT DOES AND HOW IT WORKS

Left Behind is a single, lightweight web page that tells the story of 27 NASA missions on the Moon and Mars. It opens on a 3D Moon scene with a broken lander, a rover and a flag, while the planets orbit the Sun behind it. In the 3D Explorer, visitors spin the Sun, Moon or Mars and tap glowing dots on real landing sites such as Apollo 11, Viking 1, Opportunity and Curiosity. Each mission card has three tabs: what the machine measured, the story of the mission, and the science it made possible. A status chart counts the machines (8 active, 16 dormant, 3 unknown), and a lifetime chart compares how long each Mars mission was planned to work with how long it really worked. A distance slider takes visitors out to Voyager 1, Story Mode walks through all missions in time order, and a five-question quiz tests what they learned.

BENEFITS

Anyone, even with no space background, can understand each machine in minutes. Every chapter starts with an "In simple words" box, and visitors explore at their own pace instead of reading a long page. It works on phones too: vertical swipes scroll the page and horizontal swipes rotate the 3D scene.

INTENDED IMPACT

We want people to see that "abandoned" does not mean "forgotten". By treating abandoned as a status (active, dormant or unknown) instead of an ending, the site shows that this hardware still teaches us things. For example, scientists still bounce lasers off the mirrors the Apollo crews left on the Moon. We hope to make space history more engaging and spark curiosity about humanity's presence beyond Earth.

TOOLS AND TECHNOLOGY

HTML, CSS and JavaScript. Three.js (WebGL) draws the 3D scenes, and raycasting makes the dots tappable. One shared list of missions feeds the cards, filters, charts and quiz, so a fact is fixed in one place. The solar system and stars are drawn on an HTML canvas. Facts come from public NASA mission records (NASA NSSDCA, NASA Science, NASA Mars Exploration, NASA JPL Voyager, NASA History), entered by hand. We used Claude (Anthropic) to help write code, mission descriptions and our scripts, and Google AI Studio to help generate some images. All ideas, the story structure and the final decisions are ours.

HOW IT IS CREATIVE

We turned dry mission records into small human stories: Apollo 12 astronauts walked to Surveyor 3 and took its camera home; Ingenuity was planned for 5 flights and made 72; Mars Climate Orbiter was lost because one team used imperial units and another used metric. The planned-versus-real lifetime chart makes these surprises visible at a glance.

FACTORS WE CONSIDERED

Our audience: a curious student with no space background, so we show before we explain and use plain words. Performance: one lightweight page that loads fast and needs no server. Mobile use: we fixed scroll-trapping by 3D scenes on phones. Honesty: the Moon, Mars and Sun surfaces are drawn in code, not taken from NASA photos, the planet orbits are not to scale, and the facts are hand-entered, not from a live feed. The site says so in its data notes. Next, we would connect to NASA's open data and image archives and use real imagery.
